### New-vote deferral primitive, 2026-10-28 — historical handoff

Implemented `meta::vote_admission::VoteDeferral` as an in-memory, store-instance/
representative/epoch scheduling guard. Acquisition serializes with reservations
through the existing LMDB writer, without committing a metadata row. New scalar
and batched reservations consult the same central guard; cached response checks
and a repeated existing final choice remain allowed. Existing epoch/deadline/
conflict/durable-fence checks still run, and the durable fence wins over deferral.
Nested guards reference-count ownership; drop/unwind releases only that owner.
No active guard costs one atomic read and no extra mutex/address allocation.
This is not a cross-process lock, signature authorization or persistent fence.

### Recovery caller review after152

Read-only continuation traced the actual production caller, not only the simple
rewind wrapper. `node/src/fork_resolution.rs` calls
`rollback_plan::stage_with` for admission evaluation and elected installation.
`stage_with` consumes descendant-first journals through
`rewind_block_with_snapshots` one at a time, then calls the candidate callback.
The production callback restores payment engines after that loop. A branch
containing a Merge and a verification transition therefore does not by itself
combine topology and revocation changes into one inverse journal.

When a graph inverse cannot retain the cache, `finish_trst_rewind` leaves it
absent. Later rewind iterations return early from `prepare_trst_rewind` when
that cache is absent; they do not each reconstruct all TRST state. The subsequent
`payment_transition::restore` calls `read_trst_engine`, which performs checked
wallet/graph reconstruction on a cache miss. This source trace rules out a
full-state reconstruction per remaining journal in this reviewed loop; it does
not establish a time/memory bound or prove all generic callers avoid fallback.
The public replacement callback remains general and must not be inferred safe
solely from the production callback review.

Also inspected the retained inverse's pending-basis guard: warm validation uses
`basis_validation_changes`, reverse origin/revision indexes and dirty rows.
It is not an unconditional scan of every pending row. Cold initialization still
decodes the pending table, and a large affected dependency set still costs work.
Existing `pending_revision_basis_scaling` and retained-graph recovery drivers
cover these distinct questions. Ledger reconciliation found that the same mixed
journal caller review was already recorded with the October21 pending work;
this continuation confirms that disposition rather than claiming a new fix.
The existing pending diagnostic covers100/1k/10k/100k rows: zero unrelated warm
row decodes, exactly one dirty-row decode, orphan rejection and cold reopen.
Its latest diagnostic parent is
`/home/burst/complexity-pending-revision-basis-corrected-20261021/scale-receipt.json`;
recorded100k cold construction2.053s and median warm validation0.025645ms are
historical scoped measurements, not current full-node qualification. Preparation
was already moved into startup and confirmed projection with component/node
passes. Do not schedule that implementation again. Distinct dependency fanout,
large affected sets and current full-node cold recovery remain separate gaps.
Before reusing this old result for a current claim, verify its receipt inputs;
no fresh receipt verification or runtime test was performed in this review.
No generalized inverse or new driver is justified by this trace.

## Reference simplicity review — 2026-10-25

Scope: quick source comparison of batching, rollback and storage boundaries,
not equivalence of every operation or a new production qualification.

- **Concrete avoidable work:** `trst/src/engine/holding_rows/indexed.rs`
  `with_split_revocation_cached` clones one private candidate, then invokes
  `with_replaced`/`with_inserted`, which clone its roots again for each token.
  `remove_owned` already provides the local pattern used by batched debits.
  Private insert/replace helpers can reuse that pattern while public functional
  wrappers preserve atomic failure and old snapshots. Existing rounding, order,
  shared-history and partial-failure tests should be reused. Phase145 identifies
  splitting as dominant, but does not isolate root-copy cost or prove a speedup.
- **Reference pattern:** RSNano rollback passes a single mutable write transaction
  through an explicit dependency stack and instruction executor; its block batch
  processor delegates to the ledger's existing batch operation. Reuse BURST's
  existing writer and owned candidate helpers rather than introducing another
  parallel mutation framework. RSNano's rollback semantics are not a replacement
  for BURST provenance, expiry or appeal rules.
- **Storage boundaries:** Octez separates static chain storage from versioned
  ledger contexts, with validation committing contexts. BURST already uses LMDB
  and persistent `imbl` maps. A switch to Irmin would be a migration, not a quick
  simplification. Retained rights and authenticated recovery still need their
  existing correctness checks; this comparison does not prove them unnecessary.
- **Avoidable process complexity:** per-attempt preparation/runtime scripts and
  repeated large handoffs added maintenance and fixture errors. Consolidate
  execution into existing `tools/test-node.sh` and `tools/validation-reuse.mjs`
  where supported, leaving manifests/results specific to each run. Keep one
  authoritative current narrative and short status links elsewhere when next
  restructuring documentation; preserve historical failures and receipts.
  Prefer direct stage timers for a known narrow timing question before another
  generic profiler attempt. No additional build was needed for this review.

[batch processor](https://github.com/rsnano-node/rsnano-node/blob/414dd884c162f78f151b9d912a029bbc9a340866/node/src/block_processing/block_batch_processor.rs),

## Prior handoff 135: settled Receive history lookup

Source review found a remaining CX08/CX10 amplification: `prepare_settled_token`

revision chain repeatedly. This is avoidable work beyond required chunk validation.

Historical handoff042: retirement observer contention fix PASS10storage+6node checks.
BodyChangeWatch previously held the payment-writer observer mutex across the entire
mutation callback pass (root decoding and scratch work). It now detaches rows and
the exact cut under that mutex, then runs callbacks and drops detached rows outside
it. Detached rows remain charged against the original row/byte limits. Concurrent
commits retain their images and native identities for the next visit. Callback
error/panic or committed overflow permanently invalidates coverage; aborted writes
do not. The native commit/publication lock and final cut checks remain unchanged.
This removes callback-batch work from writer lock hold time; it does not make the
required root traversal constant-time or establish measured throughput improvement.

Concrete new blocker: BodyChangeWatch::visit_commits held its mutex across every
consumer callback; payment writers acquire the same mutex in observer begin/commit.
The callbacks decode roots and write/compact scratch, so their full batch cost could
stall admission even with bounded row counts. The fix detaches rows at the checked
cut, reserves their row/byte budget until callbacks finish, retains concurrent
commits for the next visit, and poisons coverage on error/panic/committed overflow.
Native commit publication remains locked and identity-checked. No economic or
signature rule changes. This is a new production boundary, not yet qualified.

Concrete implementation order: first add bounded durable storage of *untrusted*
recovery input chunks, using the existing snapshot-page integrity/atomic-publication
pattern and scratch accounting. Reopen must verify complete extent/digest/context
metadata and reject partial/corrupt/foreign bundles. Feed reopened bytes through the
existing base/history authenticators; never deserialize an opaque authenticated
proof type. Then integrate resumable capture with explicit changed-cut handling,
bounded closure progress and deletion-writer publication checks. Retain the current
limits until the whole replacement works; a durable input cache alone does not close
R5 or remove the131072/64MiB inventory ceilings.

Cost distinction: walking a previously unauthenticated ancestry chain and checking
its signatures is required by the current head/hash-chain proof design. Persisting
raw bytes can avoid refetching and reconstruction, but is not evidence of O(1)
restart authentication. No authenticated skip-link mechanism was found in the
inspected history implementation. This review does not introduce a protocol change
or weaken signing, and does not close durable-resume or capacity gates.

R5 aggregate scratch accounting passed29focused checks (scratch-budget-20261024).
All replay temporary-file constructors now use one directory account: indexes,
variable records/sequences, recovered block bodies, snapshot bodies, canonical
sort runs and epoch sort runs. Existing live files are counted before a lease;
forks share charges. Growth reserves the complete logical extent before writing;
partial/error writes retain reservations until their file owner drops. This is
O(1) accounting per write with a shared mutex, not a filesystem quota or a measured
speedup. Filesystem allocation rounding, journal overhead and in-memory buffers
are not included. A directory-wide lease also constrains concurrent replay work
using that directory; an error defers retirement, never authorizes deletion.

Enabled retirement requires an explicit nonzero max_scratch_bytes; the default
is unset and retirement remains disabled. No invented production capacity value.
The existing small integration fixture explicitly uses64MiB. The owned async
attempt retains its lease when its caller drops the wait future, then awaits
blocking preparation/publication and existing shutdown checks.

## R5 closed-epoch signing evidence (2026-10-24)

The prior turn made verified progress on election identifiers. Further source
review found that paging alone cannot unblock retirement: all final promises,
including excluded losing forks from closed epochs, were treated as canonical
body dependencies forever. Canonical witness recovery cannot supply such forks.
`payment_epoch.rs::advance_snapshot_payment_epoch` preserves promises while
closing the old epoch; `meta.rs` rejects signing in a closed epoch. Installed
journal recovery authenticates every closure marker against forward descent
within installed certificate authority before retention pins its read view.

The root collector now uses that checked closure state to distinguish durable
signing evidence from live body dependencies. It does not delete promises or
counters. Unclosed promises still root their bodies; economic, rollback, replay,
frontier and work roots retain bodies independently. Only absence from the entire
completed dependency closure can make a certified old physical body eligible.
This also avoids requiring a nonexistent canonical witness for an excluded old
promise. Unknown, self-closing and backwards markers cannot authenticate a cut.

The existing retirement/reopen regression now includes an unavailable excluded
old promise, its authenticated closed epoch, and a live promise whose body must
remain required. Whole-metadata equality checks preserve both promises through
abort/stale/commit/reopen paths. The existing journal guard gains self, unknown-
target and backwards closure cases. This is a coherent semantic prerequisite to
resumable capacity work, not removal of inventory limits or production gating.

## Current decision table — 2026-10-24

This table is the current disposition of CX01–CX15. The finding narratives below
retain historical failures and intermediate “pending” notes; those notes are not
instructions to redo work superseded by later evidence. “Tested” means the stated
component/integration scope passed on recorded inputs, not that the entire dirty
worktree is a qualified release. Exact receipts and hashes remain in the finding
sections and [completion ledger](COMPLETION_LEDGER.md).

**Design answer:** the specs already prescribe scoped storage, expiry indexes,
merge pointers, bounded merge inputs and compute-on-read BRN. Most findings were
implementation gaps beneath that design, not missing economic design. Global
tallies, affected revocation closures and retroactive expiry changes have genuine
input-dependent costs. Neither the design nor current tests prove all resource
targets. Do not rewrite those semantics to manufacture constant-time claims.

## Focused signing and transaction-safety review — 2026-10-21

User-requested source review, separate from performance qualification. Reviewed
all 21 StateBlock variants through common authentication, operation validation,
writer-state checks and publication. Inspected existing negative-test code; no
new runtime test, penetration test or release certification is claimed here.
No unsigned-operation bypass was identified in the reviewed normal node path.
This is not a proof that every possible security defect is absent.

Common envelope: `ledger/src/state_block.rs::compute_hash` binds version, signing
grant, payment epoch, operation kind, account, predecessor, representative,
balances, link, origin, transaction, target head, timestamp, parameter hash,
merge inputs, release sources and delegation payload. Signature and PoW nonce
are excluded deliberately; work is validated separately. External full governance
content uses its committed content path rather than trusting unbound RPC text.

`node/src/block_processor/authentication.rs` recomputes the hash, validates format,
work and signature. Ordinary actions use the account public key; Epoch and
GovernanceActivation use the configured genesis key. Verification defaults to
true. The public test setter can disable it, but the repository call sites found
are test code, not a node configuration/RPC switch. Do not treat that setter or
lower-level staging helpers as independently authenticated APIs.

AuthenticatedBlock owns immutable contents and the rules used to authenticate;
admission rejects failed authentication and reauthenticates after rule changes.
It still checks current epoch, time, work, dependencies and frontier. Inside the
writer, `economic_candidate::stage` verifies the actual predecessor/account,
active signing grant and balances. `ledger_updater::predecessor_account` requires
the installed payment epoch and actual account head. Pending lookup/consumption
is recipient-keyed. Isolated economic/governance/verification candidates join one
LMDB transaction, and live roots/frontier publish only after successful commit
(`node/src/node.rs` admission commit closure). A competing branch needs the fork
path; a signature alone does not select its winner.

All rows below inherit that envelope and writer boundary. “Account” denotes the
account key, not an arbitrary key supplied by the transaction.

| Operation | Outer signer | Additional guard traced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open | Account | Zero predecessor; no invented BRN/TRST; receive-open needs actual recipient pending entry. |
| Burn | Account | Verified spending state, limits, available computed BRN; mint follows successful burn. |
| Send | Account | Verified state, limits, positive spend, transferable origin balance and exact consumed provenance. |
| Receive | Account | Recipient-keyed pending, exact amount/provenance, expiry/return-credit rules and pending consumption. |
| Merge | Account | Verified owner, bounded input list, owned selected tokens and engine composition checks. |
| Endorse | Account | Verified endorser, BRN commitment, signed target/head and lifecycle transition. |
| Challenge | Account | Verified challenger, stake and lifecycle/selection context; unsupported certified/appeal modes reject. |
| GovernanceProposal | Account | Verified proposer and validated committed content; unsupported emergency mode gated. |
| GovernanceVote | Account | Eligible voter, proposal/vote encoding and window. Delegated payload adds grant and ballot authentication. |
| Delegate | Account | Owner identity and verified eligibility; scoped grant binds network, genesis and scope. |
| RevokeDelegation | Account | Acts on signer's delegation; scoped revocation verifies owner/chain/generation authority. |
| ChangeRepresentative | Account | Predecessor and balance continuity; signed representative. |
| Epoch | Genesis | Existing target account/current head; no account action, balance or representative change. |
| RejectReceive | Account | Actual recipient pending entry; return derives from stored transfer rather than caller-invented ownership. |
| VerificationVote | Account | Certified selected voter/context, canonical choice, exact stake and parameters. |
| GovernanceActivation | Genesis | Genesis account chain, approved proposal/time and expected resulting parameters; certified mode requires its boundary. |
| VerifierOptIn | Account | Verified eligibility and own-account preference update. |
| VerifierOptOut | Account | Own-account preference update and common continuity rules. |
| GovernanceEndorse | Account | Verified supporter, open support window, exact burn and unique endorsement. |
| GovernanceWithdraw | Account | Proposal engine requires actual proposer and proposal phase/window. |
| ChangeSigner | Account | Current grant/predecessor, nonzero handoff nonce, unchanged balances/representative; successors carry new grant. |

Important distinctions: delegated ballot admission checks historical signed grant
authority; revocation/rotation determines vote weight at the certified count cut,
not arbitrary cross-account arrival order. It is not a secondary-key spending
permission. ChangeSigner changes the signing-grant identifier while authentication
still uses the account key: it must not be advertised as cryptographic revocation
of a compromised account private key.

Alternative paths reviewed: `payment_transition::authenticate_with_signer`
rechecks format/hash/signature/parameters/work; confirmed replay authenticates
contents against locally configured genesis/network history and checks grants;
fork replacement uses writer restoration/staging rather than trusting live losing
state. These helpers have different contracts; direct calls to stage/persist do
not themselves establish signature authority. Background expiry, certified
outcomes and checkpoint activation are protocol transitions, not new owner-signed
transactions, and retain their own consensus/certificate requirements.

Existing negative tests inspected include:

- `node/src/block_validation/tests.rs`: modified contents/signatures cannot reuse
  authentication; changed epoch/parameters/clock/work and signature policy are
  rechecked; preauthentication does not publish or bypass forks/gaps/release gates.
- `node/src/block_processor.rs`: wrong account signature and wrong epoch signer
  reject; open balances cannot be self-reported; forbidden balance changes reject.
- `ledger/src/state_block.rs`: payment epoch, target head, returned-stake sources
  and handoff grant/nonce are hash-bound; stale handoff grants reject.
- `node/src/payment_transition.rs`: replay rechecks signature/parameters/epoch;
  stale signer grants reject. `confirmed_replay.rs` tests trusted-genesis,
  signature, work and parameter authentication.
- Governance delegation tests cover grant generation, revocation, scope precedence
  and malformed authority; governance commit tests reject malformed proposals/
  votes, repeated or unapproved activation and duplicate support.
- Candidate staging tests cover failure isolation; pending/expiry, governance and
  verification integration evidence remains scoped as recorded in the ledger.

Conclusion: signing is present across the operation inventory and is accompanied
by substantive authorization, replay/economic and atomicity checks. This review
found no reason to say operations are accepted merely because any signature is
present. It does not establish complete adversarial coverage for every variant,
key custody/device security, network/consensus security or denial-of-service bounds.
The known complexity/resource findings remain separate; no new optimization
campaign or release approval follows from this review.

## Original result and scope — 2026-10-19

There are serious scaling problems in payment admission, governance admission,
and background expiry. The clearest superlinear payment issue is repeated vector
removal during a fragmented send. More pervasive problems are global copies,
comparisons and serialization performed for account-local operations while
holding shared engine locks and the LMDB writer.

This is a source audit of protocol revision
`f59c83e8a83283d762c41047f98a88b9589c4d8c`. It traces all 21 `BlockType` variants
through their shared admission/economic paths, with deeper inspection of payment,
governance, token provenance and their RPCs. It is not an exhaustive audit of
every function in the workspace, networking, wallet UI, consensus or snapshot
code. Fork restoration and verification are included where they amplify these
operations; their complete protocol journeys need separate profiling.

The initial 2026-10-19 review changed no production code and ran no builds,
benchmarks or acceptance. The 2026-10-20 implementation update below records
the subsequent debit, persistent-state, governance, expiry and revocation
changes and their scoped tests. Baseline findings are followed by implementation
updates; open portions remain identified. Complexity bounds follow from source
control flow and data structures; they do not establish measured latency, throughput, practical denial
of service, or a new release qualification. Existing C14 limitations in
`COMPLETION_LEDGER.md` already acknowledge global locks, detached-map comparisons
and graph-parent scans. This audit expands those limitations into actionable
operation-level findings; it does not claim those earlier optimizations failed.
The pre-existing edit to `spec/CI_REPAIR.md` was left untouched.

## Specification reconciliation — 2026-10-20

The owner had already specified the central performance architecture and targets.
The first version of this audit did not adequately trace findings to those
requirements or distinguish already-documented gaps from additional code-level
observations. These are largely implementation/conformance work under existing
requirements, not newly discovered product requirements. The source findings
remain, with the qualifications below.

Authoritative inputs reviewed for this reconciliation: `BURST_WHITEPAPER.md`,
`IMPLEMENTATION_DECISIONS.md` (actual answers, not merely bold defaults),
`spec/DECISION_RESOLUTIONS.md`, and relevant sections of `COMPLETION_PLAN.md`,
`COMPLETION_LEDGER.md` and `spec/README.md`. The latter explicitly says it does
not redefine intended functionality as a bug. This was a targeted comparison,
not a fresh full reading of every source-document section.

### Requirements already explicit

- Decisions 2.1–2.4 (`IMPLEMENTATION_DECISIONS.md:50`) select sub-second ordinary
  confirmation, 100+ TPS, under 1 GB node memory and Pi-4-class hardware. The
  audit's request to define scale must mean workload/population and measurement
  conditions; these selected performance targets must not be reopened or omitted.
- Decision 25.7 (`IMPLEMENTATION_DECISIONS.md:1977`) explicitly selects parallel
  account processing with per-account locks. C14 in `COMPLETION_PLAN.md:1111`
  already says a single atomic LMDB writer is acceptable, while serialized
  economic preparation does not meet that decision.
- Decisions 24.1, 24.4 and 24.5 select keyed durable governance/constitution state,
  efficient origin lookup and expiry indexing (`IMPLEMENTATION_DECISIONS.md:1862`).
  For 24.3 the owner delegated the general index choice; it is inaccurate to say
  the owner personally selected every suggested index there. Index existence
  alone does not prove the expensive consumer uses it efficiently.
- The whitepaper explicitly requires O(1) single-token expiry checking
  (`BURST_WHITEPAPER.md:250`) and proactive catch-time revocation followed by
  cheap validity checks (`BURST_WHITEPAPER.md:319`). Decision 6.17 expressly
  chooses merge pointers to avoid duplicating all ancestral origins and database
  growth. These are existing design constraints, not optional new optimizations.
- Decision 28.2 selects cursor pagination (`IMPLEMENTATION_DECISIONS.md:2142`).
  C17 already requires correct pagination under mutation. Encoding an offset in
  a cursor does not by itself provide stable or bounded-cost pagination.
- The storage execution plan (`COMPLETION_PLAN.md:1558`) already names detached
  map scans, parent-edge scans, full replacement and non-scoped preparation, and
  requires affected-record writes and typed durable records. The audit should
  be used as a finer-grained diagnostic under that plan, not a competing plan.

### Corrections to the recommendations

1. Preserve compute-on-read BRN (decision 5.10). Prefix integrals or exact derived
   indexes may accelerate that computation while retaining all global rate history
   and recomputing the requested balance at its timestamp. A node balance TTL or
   authoritative cached balance would change the chosen policy. Wallet caching
   was expressly allowed. CX11 is a measured-optimization candidate, not a policy bug.
2. Preserve catch-time proportional revocation and its exact rounding. The O(1)
   whitepaper claim concerns validity/expiry checks, not a complete transaction
   consuming an arbitrary number of fragments, database durability, or an entire
   electorate tally. Costs necessary to enumerate affected rights are intentional;
   global unrelated work and repeated traversal are the defects to remove.
3. The whitepaper's statement that expired/revoked history can be pruned
   (`BURST_WHITEPAPER.md:740`) needs the already-recorded qualification from
   decisions 6.9/6.15 and C16: these rights can become transferable again.
   `COMPLETION_PLAN.md:385` already reconciles that tension. Do not erase required
   ancestry/rights or flatten merge ancestry just to report lower cost.
4. Required hardware/throughput targets and per-account concurrency are already
   chosen. Future testing must specify populations and workload mixes under those
   targets. This static audit neither proves they fail at a particular size nor
   establishes that they pass.

No source whitepaper or owner decision was changed. This reconciliation changes
attribution and interpretation of the audit, not runtime code or release evidence.

## Cost model

Hash-map operations are expected O(1), not adversarial worst-case guarantees.
Map scans can depend on allocated capacity as well as populated entries. Database
point access is represented by O(log N) for an indexed table of N records;
serialized value size, page writes and durability add costs. Integer arithmetic
and fixed-size signature checks are constant with respect to ledger population.

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| W, T, t | Global wallets, global retained tokens, tokens in the affected wallet |
| B | Total BRN wallet-state size, including paused intervals and pending releases |
| G, E, H | Retained merge nodes, graph edges, revision-chain length |
| I | Size of affected global origin/holder indexes, including nested sets |
| P, V, D, C | Proposals, retained ballots, delegation records, constitution/content size |
| Sg | Whole governance/delegation/constitution serialized state size |
| U, d, q | Eligible humans, configured delegation depth, proposals requiring a tally |
| r, a, l | BRN rate segments, wallet paused intervals, pending-release records |
| k, m | Consumed send fragments, explicit merge inputs (m <= 256) |
| b, c | Pending composition portions, total settled revocation chunks |
| Q, Sv | Pending transfers and serialized verification-orchestrator size |

These dimensions are independent. A tiny block or bounded merge input does not
bound its wallet's retained tokens, the global ledger or historical governance
state. Avoid quoting a single O(1) helper as the complete operation cost.

## Findings and improvements

### CX01 — High: quadratic fragmented send (fixed in working tree, 2026-10-20)

Original source evidence: `trst/src/engine.rs:755`, `debit_wallet_with_provenance`, called by
`node/src/economic_candidate.rs:224`. Each completely consumed token invokes
`portfolio.tokens.remove(i)`. Removing near the beginning shifts the remaining
vector. Consuming k fragments from t tokens costs O(k*t), reaching O(t²) when
k is proportional to t. Provenance aggregation adds O(k), then O(b log b)
canonical sorting. The signed send names an origin, not a bounded list of
fragments; the 256-source merge limit does not bound this loop.

At t = k = 10,000, removing every first element shifts 49,995,000 token slots.
This is an arithmetic illustration, not a measured benchmark or proof of a
10,000-fragment network fixture. Repeated partial transfers/receives of the same
origin are the fixture to investigate. Global locks make the cost affect other
accounts, not just the fragmented wallet.

Fix: compact the vector in one stable pass, preserving debit order, partial
consumption, origin indexes, expiry and provenance ordering. Target O(t + b log b)
initially; an origin index can later avoid unrelated-token scans. Extend the
existing same-origin debit tests in `trst/src/engine.rs` with interspersed tokens,
partial last consumption, insufficient funds and fragmented inputs. Count visited
and moved entries in a test seam rather than relying only on wall-clock timing.

Qualification update, 2026-10-21: the signed shared-payment diagnostic now passes
all six cases (24 samples), alongside 15 focused payment regressions. Holdings are
created through signed burn/receive and self-send/receive histories, with asserted
fragment counts; the final Send consumes the entire origin. Staged results match
actual `payment_transition::apply`; aborted transactions preserve the prior head and
remove candidate block/pending writes, while committed state retains undo.

At 1/10/100/1000 consumed fragments, warm preparation ranges are
0.519–0.586 / 1.026–1.085 / 6.575–6.706 / 69.412–69.992ms in the validation profile.
At 1000 fragments, staging is 23.211–23.504ms and persistence 46.013–46.313ms;
actual reference `apply` is 72.439ms. This finite range is consistent with changed-
holding costs; timings alone do not prove asymptotic bounds. The next identified
question is persistence substage cost, separating required row deletion/undo from
avoidable repeated work. Stable holding persistence performs a retained-successor
proof, visits changed rows, encodes before/after values, checks persisted before
bytes and uses ordinary metadata writes/deletes with undo/cache hooks.

One-fragment warm preparation remains 0.552–0.590ms with 1000 synthetic unrelated
BRN records and 0.559–0.741ms with 10000; reopened cold restoration grows to 21.907ms
at 10000. This fixture supports the warm BRN reuse path, not full population or
cold-recovery qualification. Commit is timed separately (6.294–78.335ms, one per
case); parity assertions and some teardown are outside preparation. Consensus,
P2P, daily admission orchestration, release throughput and hardware memory gates
remain outside this proof. CX01 full qualification remains open.

missing and unproven cuts retain ordinary invalidation. Later unknown writes still

### CX02 — High: BRN mutations copy global wallet state

Evidence: `node/src/economic_candidate/staging.rs:38`, `brn/src/wallet_states.rs:10`,
`node/src/ledger_updater.rs:430`. First `brn_mut()` deep-clones `BrnEngine` and its
wallet map. `persist_brn_delta` subsequently compares every after-wallet and
checks every before-key. Variable-size wallet equality adds the size of interval
and release histories. A single burn therefore pays O(B), not just the cost of
one wallet's balance computation. Delta writes reduce I/O but not this CPU and
allocation cost. Building a growing population via successive mutations can
accumulate quadratic work in population.

Fix: transaction-local BRN overlays/changed-key recording with before-images,
using the existing `WalletStates` recording support where its isolation semantics
fit. Do not mutate published engines before commit. Target work proportional to
changed wallet records and their sizes, plus indexed database writes. Extend
`economic_candidate/staging/tests.rs` and BRN recording regressions; vary unrelated
wallet count while holding the touched wallet fixed.

Implementation update, 2026-10-20: BRN wallets now use a persistent ordered
map (`imbl` 7.0.2) with individually shared wallet values. Ordinary live candidate
cloning shares the tree root; lookup/mutation traverses O(log W) tree paths and
mutation copies only the touched wallet value. The existing replay recorder is
preserved, including its original capture limits. Live persistence calls a
structural diff, which skips unchanged shared subtrees and emits only semantic
insert/update/delete changes; no two explicit whole-wallet loops remain.
Independently constructed maps retain an O(W) comparison worst case. No new
recorder budget is imposed on live transactions.

Rate history and its derived accrual index are now shared too. Cloning and
unchanged-rate equality are O(1); a rate change detaches O(r) shared history,
then appends. This moves history-copy cost out of ordinary wallet mutations;
it does not make activation serialization constant-time. Wallet map aggregate
serialization now iterates in lexical address order but retains the map schema;
per-wallet rows and rate-history bytes retain their encoding. Snapshot export
still borrows wallets through a new borrowed/owned adapter and uses the existing
canonical encoder/external sort, without constructing a temporary full HashMap.

Source/API review: [imbl ordered map documentation](https://docs.rs/imbl/latest/imbl/type.OrdMap.html)
and the pinned crate's `ord/map.rs` diff implementation. The lockfile adds seven
packages without upgrading existing entries; `imbl` declares MPL-2.0+ and Rust
1.85. The resource-wrapped fetch completed; log: `/tmp/burst-complexity-imbl-fetch.log`.

`5628607b29394db6969cbba0961a5f079b893482ca0093fb691cbf307b69bcd9`).
The new 4096-wallet test checks unchanged-value sharing, candidate isolation,

### CX03 — High: TRST copy-on-write detaches whole maps

Evidence: `trst/src/shared.rs:35`, `trst/src/engine.rs:226`,
`trst/src/engine/record_delta.rs:7`, `trst/src/merger_graph.rs:119`,
`trst/src/merger_graph/records/delta.rs:5`.

Cloning a TRST snapshot is cheap. First mutation uses `Arc::make_mut`, which
clones the entire shared container. The wallet map copies W keys/shared pointers;
only the touched portfolio then copies t tokens. Holder/origin maps contain
ordinary nested sets, and merge maps contain ordinary nodes/vectors: detaching
those maps can deep-copy their accumulated contents. Delta enumeration then
scans detached maps; graph value comparisons can inspect edges/contributions.
Payment cost includes O(W + t) and whichever I/G/E structures actually detach.
It is incorrect both to call this O(1) and to claim every send copies every token
in the network. Unchanged shared maps and portfolios are skipped.

Fix: changed-key overlays, persistent map structures, or partitioned immutable
maps with explicit dirty records. Share large nested values too, but recognize
that this alone leaves a global key scan. Preserve stored-before-value conflict
checks. Extend existing record-delta and shared-snapshot tests; exercise the
first mutation after clone, not just `engine.clone()`.

Implementation update, 2026-10-20: TRST engine wallet, ownership, live-holder,
revoked-holder and outcome-invalidation maps now use persistent ordered keys
with individually shared values (`SharedMap`). Snapshot clones share tree roots;
point access/mutation traverses O(log n) keys and detaches only the affected
value. This removes copying unrelated portfolios, ownership sets and holder sets.
A touched portfolio or nested set still copies its own contents; this is not
constant-time arbitrary token mutation. `TxHash` gains bytewise ordering, without
changing encoding.

Wallet record delta discovery now uses structural map diffs and skips shared
subtrees; changed portfolios still compare position-based holding rows. Origin
moves retain the prior origin-key reconciliation and record semantics. The same
three-way undo algorithms accept either map backend through a read/mutate adapter.
Wallet snapshot serialization still explicitly sorts its records; raw map schema
is compatible. Expiry scanning collects due holders before requesting mutable
portfolios, preserving unrelated values. Finding due work is still O(W), not a
deadline index, and each due holder now has logarithmic map access.

Current holder-set update: `origin_holders` and `revoked_holders` now store
persistent `SharedSet<WalletAddress>` values inside `SharedMap`. Read-before-write
membership guards retain unchanged roots; a real membership change no longer
copies the full h-holder set. Point membership work is O(log h), in addition to
the outer map's O(log number-of-origins) access. Whole-holder enumeration and
sorting during revocation/restoration remain explicit required/retained costs.
These indexes are derived from holdings, not serialized directly. Reconstruction,
empty-set removal and sorted revocation-event ordering are preserved.
A new 4096-holder regression checks root sharing, candidate isolation, one-member
addition/removal structural diffs, exact rebuilt/restored indexes and last-member
removal. All 143 TRST tests passed (3 existing ignored), build 5.99s/runtime 2.03s.

verified local archive `target/validation-evidence/trst-holder-sets-host-20261020/host-evidence-records.tar.gz`,
SHA-256 `a1bb34c94ef50409bcd30bc3067864087b4694a37cfca525d43cd2901535ffe7`.

recorded under CX10 below. Workload qualification remains pending. Touched

### CX04 — High: one governance operation rewrites all governance state

Evidence: `node/src/node.rs:1390`, `node/src/governance_commit.rs:30`, `:101`, `:132`.
Every admitted proposal, vote, endorsement, withdrawal, delegation or revocation
restores governance, delegation and constitution. `apply` persists all three
again. Cost is at least O(Sg); delegation loading rebuilds its reverse index and
canonical serialization can add sorting. Historical proposals and votes remain
in the aggregate engine, so even a vote on a small proposal depends on unrelated
history. Repeated growth through V votes can accumulate O(V²) serialized work.
Aggregate values also enlarge undo before/after images; this can turn into a
capacity issue as well as latency.

The block path additionally calls `engines.mutable()` at `node/src/node.rs:1407`
for every governance operation, deep-cloning BRN and later scanning its wallet
map even for a vote that does not change BRN. Its TRST clone is initially cheap.
Thus the normal wrapper adds O(B) to governance operations independently of Sg.

Fix: persist proposals, ballots and delegation edges independently, with
transactional dirty keys and scoped undo. Retain historical authenticated data
outside the mutable working set without deleting replay dependencies. Request
mutable economic engines only for operations that change them. Scoped key grants
already have a bounded per-owner/scope record; avoid putting them through unrelated
aggregate work. Validate rollback, fork replacement and restart equivalence using
the existing governance commit tests before migration or candidate acceptance.

Implementation update, 2026-10-20: `GovernanceEngine` now uses persistent ordered
maps for proposals, nested exploration/promotion ballots, endorsements, timings
and secondary-key ballots. Cloning shares their roots; mutating one vote detaches
its affected map paths and proposal value instead of copying unrelated ballots.
The three pending-effect vectors still clone their contents, and touched tree
nodes can clone contained proposal values. This is not a claim that every engine
clone or mutation has zero allocation or constant total payload cost. The
previous lazy-economics change also removed the unconditional BRN/TRST candidate
request described in the baseline above.

Bincode retains the map-based field layout. A fixture with 128 proposals and
8192 exploration ballots decodes new snapshots into the old standard-map schema

Transactional storage adapter, 2026-10-20: LMDB now provides full keyed-record
initialization/read and checked delta application through its existing metadata

Rollback-scope correction, 2026-10-20: row equality alone would weaken the
legacy proposal-wide conflict rule. Two secondary ballots can change distinct
keys while belonging to the same proposal. The storage adapter now advances one
local `governance_revision/v1/<proposal>` counter per changed proposal per delta,
in the same transaction and undo journal. A later change in that scope prevents
older rewind, whereas a change in another proposal remains independent. No-op
deltas do not advance counters. Invalid/overflowing counters abort the writer.
Counters are local conflict guards, not authenticated governance values; their
namespace is deliberately separate from record reconstruction. Initialization
rejects orphaned revision rows. A typical vote/endorsement now writes two state
records plus one revision guard, rather than only two total metadata writes.

planner and migration integration still must precede a live switch. Ordinary node activation drains pending effects before persistence,
but that observation does not justify ignoring legacy snapshots/journals with
nonempty effects. Existing storage-adapter evidence must not be expanded into
migration or full rollback-compatibility qualification.

### CX05 — High: a governance read can recompute the whole governance world

Current residual source trace, 2026-10-21: bounded deadline-aware result caching
already exists and has component/HTTP evidence. The remaining confirmed issue is
whole-database generation invalidation: managed unrelated writes can republish
unchanged governance/delegation/electorate roots at a new LMDB generation, while
RPC Context clears all projected results on that new generation. This forces
recount on the next due query despite identical tally inputs. It is an avoidable
invalidation path, not evidence that all governance reads always tally or that
cache implementation is missing. A fix must carry complete input identities
through existing conservative cache invalidation and preserve time/parameter
checks, unknown-generation bypass and retention bounds. No timing claim or cache
relaxation is made by this source review; the current ledger lists required cases.

Evidence: `rpc/src/handlers/governance_projection.rs:13`,
`governance/src/projection.rs:8`, `rpc/src/handlers.rs:1814`, `:2032`,
`store_lmdb/src/account.rs:252`.

Both proposal listing and single-proposal lookup call the same full projection.
It holds governance and delegation locks, scans all account rows to construct U
verified addresses, clones the complete governance engine and visits every
proposal. Due voting phases tally every eligible person, following chains up to
d. Approximate cost is O(W + Sg + P + q*U*d), plus proposal-content copying.
Pagination happens afterwards and therefore does not bound the work. An unknown
but well-formed proposal hash also reaches projection before the not-found check.
Repeated RPC requests can contend with governance writes; actual external attack
exposure depends on deployment access controls and is not established here.

Fix: lookup/page selection first, project only requested proposals, and cache by
confirmed state identity, electorate/delegation/ballot versions and next phase
deadline. Use an indexed verified electorate. Serve immutable read snapshots
outside write-critical locks. Replace offset pagination with stable keyset
ordering; the original hash-map ordering concern was removed by the subsequent
persistent ordered-map implementation, but offset traversal remains.
Test that page size one and missing-hash requests do not tally unrelated proposals.

Implementation update, 2026-10-20: live RPC lookup now checks the requested hash
before electorate loading and projects only that proposal. Listing selects at
most page-size plus one references before projection, rather than cloning the
whole governance engine and materializing every proposal. The subsequent
persistent governance-map change now gives live proposals stable hash-key order.
It still retains the offset cursor and skips O(offset) entries; insertions or
deletions before that offset can move page boundaries. Missing hashes and empty pages do
not load the electorate or acquire the delegation lock. For nonempty requests,
an exact phase/deadline predicate avoids both when none of the selected proposals
can reach counting. The predicate reuses the support transition and stored timing;
it preserves the propagation buffer, invalid-deadline stops and rejection rules.

Keyset update, 2026-10-20: live governance now seeks strictly after the last
proposal hash through the persistent ordered map. LMDB uses an exclusive lower
bound and collects at most page-size plus one valid keys. New responses emit a
versioned `gov1:` keyset payload in the opaque cursor. Page selection costs
O(log P + page) on these paths, apart from legacy offset requests and selected
proposal projection/tally work. Existing offset cursors are accepted once and
responses switch to keysets. The generic store trait retains a sorted full-list
compatibility default; the LMDB override avoids it. The store's historical
`list_active_proposals` enumerated all valid proposal keys without filtering by
phase; this result set remains unchanged. Fallback page-read errors now propagate
instead of being hidden as an empty successful response.

CX05 read-publication trace (2026-10-20; source evidence, not a concurrency-test
result): `rpc/src/handlers/governance_projection.rs` holds governance then
delegation while reading the verified electorate and projecting selected proposals.
`node/src/node.rs` admission acquires those locks only when
`CandidateGovernance::applies_to` matches a governance/delegation block. Endorse,
Challenge and VerificationVote take the verification lock but are outside that
match. Therefore holding governance/delegation does not freeze electorate writes.
`LmdbAccountStore::iter_verified_addresses` opens its own read transaction. The
parameter helper in `rpc/src/handlers.rs` independently reads BRN metadata;
proposal-info calls it before projection, projection calls it again, and timing
is read again afterward. A cached result cannot be identified safely by just the
governance root, a wall-clock value or these mutexes. This establishes a missing
shared-snapshot contract, not an observed incorrect response or consensus failure.

The existing `LmdbReadTransaction` already pins a multi-table read view. Extend
that path rather than introducing a new writer transaction for RPC reads. Required
snapshot inputs are governance records and mode, delegation state, verified-address
index, active protocol parameters, and (for proposal-info's conflict field)
constitution state. Select the requested hash/page before loading the electorate;
missing hashes and empty pages must retain their no-tally/no-electorate behavior.

mixed-format rejection and missing/corrupt state handling. Use the pinned view's
identity for cache validity; do not tag old data with a later unlocked environment
transaction ID. A global database generation is a safe initial invalidation key
but would recreate vote-driven misses unless relevant input identities are tracked.

Capture owned persistent state/selected proposals under one read view, then close
the transaction before tallying outside engine locks. Read parameters once and
carry them with the projected proposal through response deadlines. Do not cache a
projected phase beyond its next transition or reuse it across backwards display
time. Bound retained snapshots/results; `GovernanceEngine::clone` also clones its
pending-effect vectors, so a whole-engine clone is not automatically constant-cost.
The background governance tick has the same lock-held `project_at` pattern and
needs the same input contract; optimizing only RPC would leave that writer blocker.

Evidence: `governance/src/engine.rs:1124`, `governance/src/delegation.rs:202`,
`governance/src/ballot.rs:131`,

Ordinary counting builds an eligible set and follows up to d links per eligible
wallet: O(U*d), not unconditionally O(U²). Certified electorate commitment also
uses a BTreeSet: O(U log U). Key delegation projection clones delegation state,
then repeatedly restores scoped grants along each chain. Scoped restore calls
`DelegationAuthority::restore`, which verifies grants, so shared chain prefixes
repeat cryptographic work as well as lookup work. Each scope is capped at 2048
bytes; traversal respects the engine depth setting (default 10, not a universal
restoration cap; see qualification below). These are meaningful protections.

Fix: cache authenticated scope records and resolved suffixes within one immutable
counting cut, accounting for remaining depth, cycles, eligibility, proposal-over-
parameter precedence, direct-vote overrides and explicit revocations. Reuse the
electorate commitment within the same authenticated cut. Do not cache across
history/parameter changes or silently remove the depth rule. Existing delegation,
ballot and key-delegation tests are the regression base.

Implementation update, 2026-10-20: `delegation_at_cut` now lazily caches the
resolved, authenticated scoped grant for each visited owner. The cache belongs
to one immutable proposal/metadata counting cut and is discarded afterward.
It distinguishes absence (legacy fallback) from an explicit revocation (no
fallback), and caches both. Scope precedence is still resolved by the existing
proposal-before-parameter lookup. Malformed records fail at their first reached
lookup, without eagerly inspecting unrelated metadata.

Each reached owner's selected record is decoded/authenticated at most once per
cut, rather than once per shared-chain visit. With V distinct visited owners,
cryptographic restore work is O(V) bounded scope records; traversal remains
O(U*d), with O(V) additional cache memory. Eligibility, visited-set/cycle checks,
remaining depth, recipient checks and ballot lookup still execute per hop.
Delegation-engine cloning, suffix traversal, repeated recipient/id derivation
and electorate commitment work remain; CX06 is not fully closed.

| Reuse candidate | Safe condition in the immutable cut | Required counterexample/regression |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Completed suffix with effective vote | Retain distance to the first vote; accept only within remaining hop budget | Same suffix queried with shorter/longer budgets and opposite owner orders |
| Completed suffix stopped by absent/revoked scope or ineligible recipient | Preserve the outer owner's absent-scope legacy fallback separately | Root absent versus upstream absent, explicit revocation, recipient invalid before ID |
| Completed cycle with no vote | No effective ballot was encountered before repetition | Vote before cycle closure, self-cycle, incoming tail |
| Depth-exhausted prefix | May cache only the explored horizon; must not turn it into an unconditional no-vote suffix | Later owner with more remaining depth reaches a ballot beyond the first query's horizon |
| Unevaluated metadata beyond a horizon | Must remain unevaluated until demanded by an actual query | Malformed scope/ID and fixed original voter order/error precedence |

covering no-vote chains as well as shared successful tails. Caching only successful
votes improves favorable cases but leaves the worst-case finding open. Review the
prefix-composition bound before implementing; a cache keyed by every remaining
depth can still grow to O(V*d). Do not trade a linear scan for that memory growth
without measurement and an explicit bound. Decisions 20.6–20.8 require concurrent,
revocable transitive proposal/parameter delegation, not a new depth cap.

### CX07 — High: every expiry tick scans all held tokens even with no expiry

Evidence: `node/src/node.rs:2344`, `node/src/expiry_commit.rs:7`,
`node/src/ledger_updater.rs:19`, `trst/src/engine.rs:1755`.

Every 60 seconds the worker takes the TRST lock and starts a writer. Although
`flush_all_expired` skips individual portfolios with no due expiry, `stage`
unconditionally refreshes counters for every holder. That loops over all T
tokens and attempts account updates for W holders even if no token expired.
Noncertified mode additionally materializes and scans Q pending transfers;
certified `apply_held` deliberately does not return pending payments on local time.
Idle work is therefore O(W + T), plus database operations, or more when pending
returns are enabled. Existing expiry-index cleanup does not remove this scan.

Fix: track next due wallet/token deadlines and update only affected counters.
Maintain a pending expiry index where the certified boundary permits returns.
Use the existing changed-holder expiry helper as a starting point, not a complete
solution: it still scans wallets. Preserve resurrection when governance changes
the expiry period and distinguish held display expiry from certified ownership
returns. Extend `expiry_commit` tests with no-due and one-due large-state cases.

Implementation update, 2026-10-20: the TRST engine now maintains a derived
persistent deadline schedule and a shared wallet-root baseline. Before each
flush, structural diff discovers portfolios changed since the preceding refresh;
only those deadlines are replaced. Unchanged shared subtrees are skipped. The
ordered deadline prefix selects due wallets; the returned holder list is sorted
by address to preserve the prior flush-result order. The schedule synchronizes
again after flushing, so the next idle tick does not rediscover expired entries.
All wallet mutation paths, including direct shared-map edits, are reconciled
through the baseline diff rather than relying on a new caller-maintained dirty
flag. The index is not serialized or balance authority; restart builds it from
existing portfolio deadlines. Governed resurrection still uses the established
full normalization and its changed portfolios update the schedule.

Cold initialization is O(W log W) deadline insertion. Warm refresh is structural
diff plus changed portfolio equality and O(log W) deadline updates per changed
holder; independent reconstructed maps retain a global diff worst case. Due work
includes O(D log D) result ordering and the existing affected-portfolio token
scans. An unchanged idle engine no longer enumerates all holders; locating the
due prefix still has tree-iterator setup cost. Additional memory is O(W) index
entries and a shared prior root, which can retain previous versions of changed
portfolio values until synchronization. It is not a guarantee of O(W) total bytes
independent of token state. Candidate clones share the schedule as well.

The node still refreshes all holder counters and scans pending returns in the
legacy path; therefore the overall idle-node O(W+T) finding remains open. Simply
filtering by changed token state needs a separate proof: counter computation uses
the current time even for already-expired holdings, and time can move backward.
Do not remove this behavior without accounting for clock and account-counter
updates. Certified ownership returns remain unchanged.

### CX08 — Medium: wallet token lookup, insertion and storage position amplify work

Evidence: `node/src/economic_candidate.rs:265`, `:308`,
`trst/src/engine.rs:142`, `:541`, `:626`, `:687`,
`trst/src/engine/record_delta.rs:33`.

Explicit merge selection does a linear token search for each of m inputs:
O(m*t). Automatic merge sorts all live wallet tokens before taking at most 256:
O(t log t), O(t) temporary references. Bulk removal is a good single retain pass,
but deindexing then scans the remaining portfolio once per removed origin/tag.
The m cap limits the multiplier, not t. Candidate send balances and per-block
expired/revoked counters also scan t. Even preference-only accepted blocks invoke
`refresh_token_counters` when a portfolio exists.

Tokens are stored in a vector and persisted by position. Receiving an old token
can shift O(t) entries in memory and make O(t) holding rows appear changed.
Delivering b portions and c revoked chunks can cause repeated sorted insertions,
up to O((b+c)*t + (b+c)²) moves in an adverse ordering. Basis checks can also walk
revision chains (CX10). Ordinary latest-timestamp append remains efficient.

Fix: stable token-ID storage plus a separate ordered index; per-wallet token-ID,
origin and live-origin counts; bounded top-k selection or an ordered expiry index
for automatic merge. Bulk merge received sorted runs instead of individual inserts.
Cache/update counters from changes and scheduled expiry. Preserve deterministic
selection and token identity. Test out-of-order receive and front-of-vector deletion
against persisted delta row counts, not just emitted economic balances.

Stable codec foundation implemented and unit-qualified (not active storage):
`trst::engine::holding_rows` uses a separate `trst_holdings/v2/` namespace. A header
stores head/count/caches; rows keyed by holder/token ID carry next-token links.
This preserves equal-timestamp sequence independently of ID ordering. Key/version/
owner binding, row size limits, duplicate IDs, malformed/cyclic/disconnected links,
counts, cached balances and governed expiry are checked. Declared count does not
control allocation. Decoding is not ledger authentication or publication authority.

Four focused tests passed (compile 6.22s, tests 0.65s; receipt checked). At 32/256/
1024 holdings, front insert/delete changes two portfolio rows, append/tie insertion
and middle/tail deletion three, payload amount change two. Delta CAS application
matches full stable encoding and restores byte-identical canonical portfolios;
empty/absent distinction, tie order and reverse deltas are covered. This fixes the
representation's write amplification, but it is not wired into LMDB or activated.
Delta computation still costs O(old+new holdings) time and O(old holdings) temporary
lookup memory; output allocation is proportional to changed rows. Vec COW/movement
also remains. All origin/provenance records and economic token fields are unchanged.

### CX08 historical hot-path trace before retained engine/cache integration

This retained historical trace motivated the indexed engine/cache work below. Several
rows describe costs since removed on eligible retained paths; use the current
operation map and ledger for current status. Optimizing `visit_delta` alone
cannot make a small payment scale with only changed holdings. Let t be one wallet's
holdings, k its changed holdings, q holdings relevant to the selected origin, and N
all holdings. These are source-derived costs, not new timing measurements.

| Boundary / operation | Current source and remaining cost | Required work versus avoidable work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Candidate first mutation | `shared.rs::Shared::deref_mut` uses `Arc::make_mut`; `WalletPortfolio::clone` clones its public token Vec | Preserving the old cut is required; copying every unrelated token in that wallet is avoidable with persistent per-holding storage. Outer wallet-map persistence alone does not solve this. |
| Append / receive | `track_token` updates caches and inserts into Vec; `receive_settled_batch` splices an ordered run | New tokens and origin registration are required. Shared-vector detachment and out-of-order shifts remain O(t), even when stable storage changes only a few rows. |
| Admission origin balance | `candidate_balances` scans all tokens even when no expiry flush is due; `origin_transferable` filters all tokens | Exact per-origin balance and nonmutating admission are required. Unrelated-origin scans are avoidable through maintained origin aggregates and expiry-aware indexes. |
| Origin debit | `debit_wallet_with_provenance` retains/mutates the ordered token vector; holder deindex checks scan remaining tokens | Examining consumed portions and preserving oldest-first/tie order and provenance is required. Scanning unrelated origins and rescanning for last membership are avoidable; index both order and origin membership/counts. |
| Single/bulk untrack | `untrack_token` linearly locates and removes; `bulk_untrack` retains across the full vector and may recompute expiry | Removing requested IDs is required. ID lookup, shifts and full minimum recomputation need per-ID/order/expiry structures; bulk work remains at least proportional to affected holdings. |
| Explicit merge selection | `merge_selection::select_merge_inputs` scans holdings once and returns signed input order | The <=256 signed IDs must be checked with duplicates still rejected. A maintained ID index can replace the O(t) search with point lookups. |
| Automatic merge selection | `select_expiry_merge_group` scans t using a bounded heap | The existing effective-timestamp, ID, position tie rule and expiry cutoff must remain exact. This ordering is different from the portfolio's origin-timestamp order; one ordered index cannot silently substitute for both. |
| Expiry / revocation | Due-wallet schedule skips idle wallets, but `flush_expired`, whole-origin revocation and proportional split scan the wallet | Processing affected tokens and prescribed catch-time splitting is required. Unrelated-token scans inside affected wallets need token-level expiry/origin indexes; pointer-graph ancestry and rounding stay unchanged. |
| Governance expiry period | `set_expiry_period` examines N tokens and can resurrect Expired holdings | This may legitimately affect N holdings and output O(N) changes. An incremental index must not freeze expiry at insertion or claim O(1) for a whole-governance transition. |
| Stable write delta | `holding_rows::visit_delta` validates complete before/after vectors and matches IDs | Cold/untrusted input validation is required. Rechecking unchanged holdings on every trusted mutation is avoidable only after establishing an immutable validated root and checked update API. Current public mutable values do not establish that proof. |
| Warm writer-cache refresh | `AuxiliaryCache::update_trst` records only dirty holders. `read_trst_engine` then calls `read_trst_portfolio` for each and `RestoredTrstState::replace_records` | A two-row stable update still reloads/reconstructs the entire touched wallet on the next cached read. Exact storage-cut consistency is required; a validated per-row patch with local link/cache proofs is needed to remove that O(t) read/validation work. |
| Cold restore / full snapshot | `WalletRecordReader`, `holding_rows::restore`, `RestoredTrstState::from_engine` validate serialized state | Full input decoding and duplicate/order/link/count/cache/ownership checks are intentional O(input) work. Persistent indexes must be derived only after these checks; stable rows do not replace authentication/finality. |

The current safe reuse boundaries are narrower than a general validation cache:

- `Shared<WalletPortfolio>` has immutable root identity until mutable access detaches
  it. The existing weak-root counter cache correctly invalidates on mutation; it can
  reuse the same cut but supplies neither a token delta nor proof for a new cut.
- `TrstEngine::wallets`, `WalletPortfolio::tokens` and the aggregate fields are public;
  `get_portfolio_mut` also returns unrestricted mutable access. A boolean “validated”
  flag carried by Clone would become stale unless every such route invalidates it.
  Root identity alone proves unchanged data, not that it ever passed validation.
- `RestoredTrstState` owns a validated engine and exposes immutable borrowing, but
  `replace_portfolio` still validates and indexes a full portfolio. `into_engine`
  returns the general mutable engine; callers cannot retain the old proof for it.
- Graph, invalidation, format and governed-period writes currently invalidate the
  storage cache globally. A row-patch fast path must retain that fallback, account
  for arbitrary preceding writes in the same transaction, and publish only at the
  same commit/abort boundary. Installing the caller's proposed `after` engine solely
  because a few row CAS checks passed would not prove untouched state is consistent.

Implementation requirements for the next coherent boundary:

1. Keep canonical Vec serialization and current row keys/links as compatibility
   boundaries, while introducing a private immutable validated holding root. Reuse
   the existing persistent-map machinery rather than another pointer cache. A cold
   conversion may remain O(t); warmed checked updates must avoid cloning the full Vec.
2. Maintain ID lookup, exact portfolio order, active balance, expiry minimum and
   origin/revocation membership together. Preserve restored arbitrary tie order and
   append-after-existing-ties behavior. Sorting equal timestamps by token ID would
   change current semantics. Any private order labels need a non-economic overflow
   recovery path and must not alter snapshot bytes or token identities.
3. Make checked mutation return a new root plus only changed token/link/header rows;
   reject duplicate IDs and arithmetic overflow before publication. Keep a fully
   validating fallback for raw snapshot/row input and unrestricted legacy mutations
   until those APIs have been migrated. A fallback must be explicit in measurements.
4. Feed those verified row changes through existing bounded journal callbacks and
   exact CAS, and patch the writer's validated root from the same transactional cut.
   Verify link endpoints, count, cache summaries, origin registration and period
   dependencies; a changed-row-only CAS is not a proof of the whole portfolio.
5. Measure end-to-end candidate preparation, delta generation, writer cache refresh
   and snapshot retention separately at 1k/10k/100k. Reuse existing migration, undo,
   corruption and tie-order oracles; add root-sharing/visited-node assertions and
   mixed legacy-write invalidation coverage. Node release/TPS/memory gates remain
   separate. Do not rerun the unchanged 96ms probe merely to restate this trace.

This is implementation work under Decisions 24.3–24.5 and the preserved TRST rules,
not a change to the whitepaper. No persistent portfolio or incremental cache patch
is claimed implemented by this source trace. The measured 64% improvement remains
valid for its exact inputs; the remaining common-operation regression stays open.

Persistent-root implementation update: `holding_rows::indexed::IndexedPortfolio`
now implements the first structural boundary above. Its private persistent ID/order/
active-expiry maps support checked immutable insert/replace/remove with shared token
payloads, checked balance updates, duplicate rejection and exact expiry minima. Cold
conversion checks canonical state once; canonical export remains O(t). Restored tie
order survives, insertion follows existing ties, and private order-label exhaustion
relabels without changing economic identity. Point updates use O(log t) index work;
exhaustion recovery/cold construction cost O(t log t). The visitor skips shared branches
and streams header then token-ID-ordered changed rows. Its output order differs from
legacy portfolio traversal and must be accounted for during integration.

Storage redesign constraints from current source:

* `WalletRecord::Holding` binds `(holder, position)` to `trst_state/v1/` keys, and
  `WalletRecordReader` requires contiguous positions. `visit_wallet_records` also
  emits this canonical order for snapshots; changing a key alone is insufficient.
* `WalletPortfolio::validate_snapshot` rejects duplicate token IDs, so stable ID
  keys are compatible with valid restored holdings. `track_token` itself does not
  reject duplicates; a new encoder must not silently overwrite an invalid duplicate.
* Equal origin timestamps retain arrival/insertion order. Sorting by token hash
  would alter existing selection/tie semantics. Identity and order must be separate.
* `node::trst_storage::persist_delta` compares old bytes before each mutation and
  rejects primary-key changes in a paired delta. Preserve these conflict checks.
* `trst_storage::migrate` atomically converts provisional journals and holdings,
  validates ledger completeness, bounds journals (131,072 records / 64 MiB), sets
  the format marker, commits and force-syncs. Existing conversion understands
  aggregate snapshots to positional v1, not a prospective stable-key layout.
* `stage_replayed`, LMDB scoped readers/cache dirty tracking, block-undo metadata
  handling, and certified snapshot installed/recorded changes depend on v1 record
  namespaces. They must be reviewed together; an ordinary persistence-only change
  would leave recovery incompatible.

Candidate design to evaluate: keep canonical snapshot token order unchanged, but
use a separately versioned local storage representation keyed by `(holder, token_id)`
with an explicit order representation (for example head plus next-token links).
A front insertion then changes its new row and ordering metadata rather than every
suffix key. Such links require strict duplicate/missing/cycle/disconnected/count
validation and atomic neighbor/header updates. They must reproduce the exact prior
sequence, including ties, and must not enter economic identity merely as storage
implementation data. The linked representation is now implemented as the unactivated codec above;
its database/migration integration remains unproven. A v2 design also needs reversible
provisional undo conversion and snapshot/replay compatibility tests before activation.
Reducing durable rows alone would not remove current Vec COW, shifting, or O(t)
comparison; those remain separate implementation work under the original objective.
Decisions 6.12, 6.17 and 24.3–24.5 do not require positional primary keys, and this
redesign must preserve the merge cap and transaction-pointer provenance model.

Evidence: `node/src/graph_storage/delta.rs:35`,
`trst/src/merger_graph/records/delta.rs:70`.

The first appended edge for each parent in a transaction scans its stored edge
prefix to find the maximum position. In-memory delta handling checks old-prefix
equality and recounts child occurrences over the parent's full vector. One append
to a parent with e edges takes O(e) work before the write, in addition to CX03.
n successive extensions of a popular parent can accumulate O(n²) work. The
per-transaction highest-position cache helps multiple appends in one batch, not
successive blocks.

Fix: transactional next-position/occurrence indexes, or a proven ordered range
tail lookup for positions. Journal these indexes and validate/migrate existing
rows. A recorded appended-edge list can eliminate repeated prefix comparisons.
Extend `graph_storage/tests` with repeated parent extension and rollback/reopen.

Implementation constraint confirmed, 2026-10-20: `graph_storage/delta.rs` scans
stored parent rows because durable positions survive disjoint merge undo and can
have gaps. The in-memory vector length is not the durable maximum. Any tail index
must preserve that property, old-row conflict checks, shared-parent rollback and
full replacement/import behavior. A naive length-based counter is not equivalent.

Durable position index implementation, 2026-10-20: schema 5 adds the derived
`graph_positions` database, ordered by edge kind, parent and big-endian position.
Existing schema 3/4 rows rebuild into this index in one atomic open transaction,
using batches of at most 256 decoded edge rows; governance conversion remains a
separate operation. Older schema-4-only binaries reject schema 5. A schema-5
store missing the index database is rejected, not silently recreated empty.
Batched and direct metadata writers maintain index entries with primary rows.
Undo journals still contain only primary edges, so two merges sharing a parent
acquire no new shared journal conflict. Prefix replacement deletes through the
same hooks; complete metadata replacement clears the derived index as well.

`graph_storage::persist_delta` now seeks the greatest surviving durable position
and validates the selected index entry against its primary row, then uses the
existing transaction-local position cache. This removes the persisted O(e) parent
scan; the B-tree seek/update costs O(log E). Gaps, repeated children, overflow and
surviving journal positions retain their semantics. In-memory vector detachment,
prefix equality and occurrence recounts remain unresolved; CX09 is not closed.

In-memory append implementation underway, 2026-10-20: each parent now owns a
persistent ordered map of positions to (child, occurrence) plus a persistent map
of child counts. Candidate clones share those roots; appending changes paths in
both trees. Ordinary delta generation compares the position trees, skipping shared
subtrees and rejecting deletes/replacements/noncontiguous additions. Each emitted
edge already has its occurrence number; prior children are not recounted. Parent
lookup remains logarithmic in parent count; per-parent append is logarithmic in
its edge/unique-child counts. Full export still visits all edges as required.

Snapshot encoding writes only the original child sequence with its original length;
derived counts never enter the wire layout. Decode rebuilds trees and counts and
therefore costs O(e(log e + log u)) to reconstruct e edges with u unique children
under a parent, instead of a flat Vec decode. Three-way undo borrows input sequence
iterators, but rebuilding a changed surviving parent also incurs that tree
construction cost; its prior global validation/traversal remains. This cold/rewind
tradeoff must be included in qualification rather than hidden by warm append results. New regressions
exercise 4096 existing edges, repeated-child suffix occurrences, shared roots,
legacy Vec bytes and rejection of truncation/reordering/replacement. The desktop
resource wrapper refused before compilation (<4GiB available); its incomplete
receipt is retained. First capped VM1 compile failed E0311 before tests: the
borrowed sequence trait needed an explicit item lifetime. Matching trait/impl
bounds are now corrected; the suite under `complexity-edge-list-20261020/engine-fix/`

test covers correctness, not timed persisted high-fanout admission. Extend the

driver. Do not infer that the cold-reader allocations caused the whole RSS peak.

### CX10 — High potential lifecycle spike: revocation multiplies graph and history work

Evidence: `trst/src/engine.rs:1124`, `:1185`, `:1234`, `:1349`,
`trst/src/merger_graph.rs:304`, `:368`, `:420`.

Revocation correctly uses origin-holder indexes and an affected DAG closure;
it does not blindly visit all holders or recursively enumerate every path.
However, it repeats propagation per burn origin of the challenged wallet.
Overlapping affected closures therefore repeat graph work. Each affected
origin/merge holder then scans that holder's portfolio, so one wallet holding
many affected origins can incur repeated t-sized scans.

Split-insertion update, 2026-10-20: `split_revoke_tokens` previously collected
chunks in token timestamp order, then inserted each separately, potentially
shifting a newer tail for every chunk. `insert_sorted_run` now merges those chunks
in O(t+c) token movement. Existing tokens precede new equal-timestamp chunks,
and chunk order remains stable. Empty/append/equal-timestamp paths avoid a general
merge; interleaving allocates an O(t+c) output buffer, so this is not a lower
peak-memory claim. Cached balance subtraction, provenance cuts, event emission
and index changes are untouched. A differential regression compares sequential
insertion across 45 empty/single/many and timestamp arrangements. All 144 TRST
library tests passed, including existing split/revocation/undo tests and the new
persistent holder-set regression (build 5.96s/runtime 2.01s). Receipt:

Original finding (the source-position and per-transition history fixes are implemented
below): `compute_taints` linearly searched source revisions for each immediate
source, allowing O(m²) per node with m bounded at 256. A remainder lookup walked
up to H revisions. The original bound included affected vertices/edges, per-node
m², repeated revision traversals, holder sorting and affected portfolio scans. This is not simply O(number of affected
tokens), and repeated revocation/restoration can grow H. `revoked_total` also
sums the node's contribution map each time it is requested.

Fix: index source revisions by source position, memoize immutable revision
queries per transition, cache checked contribution totals, and group affected
work by holder where the exact rounding/event order permits. Explore a combined
multi-origin traversal only with a proof that sequential rounding and appeal
reversal remain identical. Preserve live/pending distinctions and authenticated
history; blindly pruning revisions breaks old composition bases. Extend existing
multi-origin, split, appeal and outcome-revocation tests before scale profiling.

Implementation update, 2026-10-20: `compute_taints` now builds a source-position
lookup once per affected merge. For m immediate inputs and r stored revision rows,
basis discovery costs O(m+r) time and O(m) temporary slots rather than O(m*r).
First-match behavior is preserved for duplicate/raw rows, including explicit
`Entire` entries; out-of-range rows remain irrelevant to input positions. The
normal 256-input limit is unchanged. Source order, taint accumulation, saturation,
rounding and final total cap are unchanged.

The same traversal keeps an origin-specific revision memo. Each newly visited
revision records the nearest matching origin's revoked/restored answer, including
negative answers. Later queries sharing that suffix reuse the result. For R
visited revisions, history lookup work is O(R log H) for the persistent revision
map plus expected constant-time memo accesses, rather than repeatedly walking
shared histories. Temporary memory is O(R), and the cache is discarded before
the graph can change or a different origin is processed. Other `revoked_at`
callers retain their existing behavior; this is not a global history cache.
